overview.title: Top-class prediction and splitting Xception for Grad-CAM
overview.main_topic: Reading the classifier's top-five predictions for the elephant image, finding the top class index (386, African elephant), preprocessing the image explicitly with the task's preprocessor, and starting to cut the model into two submodels: input -> last convolutional activations (Listing 10.18) and last convolutional activations -> class predictions (Listing 10.19, continued on p.326).
overview.central_idea: To get the gradient of the class score with respect to the last convolutional feature map, the model is split at layer block14_sepconv2_act into a feature-map model and a classifier model. Because these submodels bypass the task's built-in preprocessing, the image must first be passed through model.preprocessor.
overview.importance: Splitting the network makes the last conv output an explicit tensor that can be watched by a gradient tape or differentiated by jax.grad (p.326-p.327). Getting the split and the preprocessing right is the practical heart of the Grad-CAM implementation.
learning_objectives: Interpret the top-five ImageNet predictions and the argmax index 386.
Explain why the image must be preprocessed manually with model.preprocessor before using the submodels.
Build a Keras functional model that outputs an intermediate layer's activations (last_conv_layer_model).
Explain why the last convolutional layer is chosen as the place to split the model.
Begin a second model whose input is the last conv layer's output (classifier_input).
prerequisites: The ImageClassifier task and its predictions (p.324)
Extracting intermediate activations with keras.Model(inputs, layer.output), as in section 10.1 (p.310-p.312)
The Grad-CAM idea of weighting channels by class gradients (p.323)

summary:
The page first finishes the prediction output from p.324: the last two decoded entries are `("triceratops", 0.00029)` and `("Mexican_hairless", 0.00018)`. The text then lists the **top five classes**: African elephant (90%), tusker (5%), Indian elephant (2%), and triceratops and Mexican hairless dog (each under 0.1%).

The network has recognized "an undetermined quantity of African elephants" (the classifier says *what* is in the picture, not how many). The maximally activated entry of the prediction vector is **index 386**, the African elephant class: `np.argmax(preds[0])` returns `386`.

The goal now is to see which parts of the image are the most "African elephant-like", so the Grad-CAM process is set up:

- **Preprocessing.** We did not preprocess the image before calling the task, because `ImageClassifier` preprocesses inputs inside `predict()`. For Grad-CAM we will call parts of the network directly, so we preprocess ourselves: `img_array = model.preprocessor(img_array)` (callout: KerasHub tasks have a preprocessor layer).
- **Listing 10.18.** A model that maps the input image to the activations of the last convolutional layer: the layer `"block14_sepconv2_act"` is fetched from `model.backbone` with `get_layer()`, and `keras.Model(model.inputs, last_conv_layer.output)` creates `last_conv_layer_model`.
- **Listing 10.19 (begins).** A second model maps those activations to the final class predictions. It starts with `classifier_input = last_conv_layer.output` and `x = classifier_input`; the rest (applying the `pooler` and `predictions` layers) is on p.326.

Splitting the network at the last conv layer turns its output into an explicit input of the classifier part, which is exactly the tensor we need gradients with respect to.

paragraphs.excerpt: The top five classes predicted for this image are as follows:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduces a bulleted list of the top five predictions: African elephant (90%), tusker (5%), Indian elephant (2%), and triceratops and Mexican hairless dog with less than 0.1% each.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The percentages are rounded versions of the decoded probabilities: 0.90331, 0.05487, 0.01637, 0.00029 and 0.00018. Almost all probability is on elephant classes; the last two are tiny residuals.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It confirms the model classifies the image correctly, so the heatmap we are about to build explains a correct decision for the class African elephant.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 'tusker' is an ImageNet class for elephants with prominent tusks, which the adult in Figure 10.7 has; its 5% share is a plausible confusion rather than an error.

terminology.meaning: The five classes with the highest predicted probabilities.

connections: p.324: the decoded output began with African_elephant 0.90331, tusker 0.05487, Indian_elephant 0.01637.

paragraphs.excerpt: The network has recognized the image as containing an undetermined quantity of African
paragraphs.what_it_says: The network recognized the image as containing an undetermined number of African elephants. The maximally activated entry of the prediction vector corresponds to the African elephant class at index 386, as shown by np.argmax(preds[0]).
paragraphs.what_it_means: An image classifier outputs one distribution over classes per image; it says nothing about how many instances there are. The argmax index identifies which of the 1,000 output units we will explain.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The 'top class' used in the gradient code on p.326-p.327 is exactly this argmax (computed there with ops.argmax(preds[0])). Grad-CAM produces a heatmap for one class at a time.
paragraphs.technical_idea: preds[0] selects the first (only) image in the batch, giving a vector of 1,000 probabilities; np.argmax returns the position of its largest entry.

terminology.meaning: The index of the maximum value in an array.
The model's 1,000 class probabilities for one image.

connections: p.326: Listing 10.20 recomputes top_pred_index = ops.argmax(preds[0]) inside the gradient tape.
p.143: argmax was used to read multiclass predictions in the newswire example.

paragraphs.excerpt: To visualize which parts of the image are the most African elephant–like,
paragraphs.what_it_says: The next step is to set up the Grad-CAM process to show which parts of the image are the most African elephant-like.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The question shifts from 'what is in the image?' (answered by the classifier) to 'where in the image is the evidence for that answer?'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sentence frames everything through p.330: the output will be a spatial map for the single class African elephant.
connections: p.323: Grad-CAM produces a spatial map of 'how intensely the input image activates the class'.

paragraphs.excerpt: You will note that we didn’t need to preprocess our image before calling
paragraphs.what_it_says: We did not preprocess the image before calling the task model because the KerasHub ImageClassifier preprocesses inputs as part of predict(). We now preprocess the image ourselves so we can use the preprocessed inputs directly, with img_array = model.preprocessor(img_array).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The submodels about to be built start at the backbone's input, after the preprocessing stage. Calling them on raw pixels would feed the network data at the wrong scale and size. Applying model.preprocessor once gives exactly what the backbone expects.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A silent bug source: if preprocessing is skipped, the heatmap is computed for an input the network never sees in normal use, and the gradients and predictions change. If it is applied twice (manually and again inside predict()), the input is also wrong.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The preprocessor is itself a layer (callout: 'KerasHub tasks like ImageClassifier have a preprocessor layer'), so it can be called like a function on a batch of images. Beyond the book: for Xception it resizes the image to the model's input resolution and rescales pixel values to the range used during pretraining.

terminology.meaning: The task's preprocessing layer (resizing and rescaling for images) that predict() applies automatically.

connections: p.317: section 10.2 also stressed applying model-specific preprocessing so images match the Xception pretraining range.
p.282: ImageConverter handles the [0, 1] vs [-1, 1] input range of different pretrained models.

paragraphs.excerpt: First, we create a model that maps the input image to the activations
paragraphs.what_it_says: The first submodel maps the input image to the activations of the last convolutional layer (Listing 10.18).
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the 'feature map' half of Grad-CAM: for the given image it yields a tensor of shape (1, rows, cols, channels) whose channels are the high-level features we will weight.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The last convolutional layer is used because it is the deepest layer that still has spatial structure: deep enough to encode class-relevant concepts, but not yet pooled away into a single vector.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: for Xception the layer block14_sepconv2_act (the ReLU after the final separable convolution) outputs 2,048 channels on a coarse grid (10 x 10 for a 299 x 299 input). That coarse grid is why the heatmap in Figure 10.8 is blocky.

terminology.meaning: The final layer with a spatial (rows x cols) output before global pooling.

connections: p.310: section 10.1 built a model returning intermediate activations in the same way.

paragraphs.excerpt: Second, we create a model that maps the activations of the last convolutional
paragraphs.what_it_says: The second submodel maps the last convolutional layer's activations to the final class predictions (Listing 10.19, which starts on this page and finishes on p.326).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Splitting the network lets us treat the last conv output as an ordinary input tensor of the classifier part, so we can compute the derivative of the class score with respect to it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Differentiating with respect to an intermediate activation is easiest when that activation is the input of a function. The two submodels compose back into the full classifier: classifier_model(last_conv_layer_model(x)) equals the original prediction.

terminology.meaning: The symbolic tensor last_conv_layer.output, reused as the input of the second model.

connections: p.326: the head layers 'pooler' and 'predictions' are applied to x and classifier_model is created.

concepts.name: Grad-CAM
concepts.definition: Class activation mapping that weights the channels of a convolutional feature map by the gradient of a class score with respect to those channels.
concepts.intuition: Find the channels that matter for the class, then see where in the image those channels fire.
concepts.technical: Requires the feature map of the last conv layer and the gradient of the top class score with respect to it; this page sets up the first of these and begins the model for the second.
concepts.significance: Explains why the network predicted African elephant and where it looked.
concepts.example: Top class index 386 (African elephant) for the test image.
concepts.misconception: Grad-CAM does not count objects; neither does the classifier ('an undetermined quantity').

concepts.name: Splitting a model at an intermediate layer
concepts.definition: Building one model from the original input to an intermediate layer's output, and a second model from that output to the final prediction.
concepts.intuition: Cutting a pipe in two so you can measure what flows through the cut.
concepts.technical: keras.Model(model.inputs, last_conv_layer.output) gives the first half; a second keras.Model takes last_conv_layer.output as input and reapplies the remaining layers (p.326).
concepts.significance: Makes the intermediate activation an explicit tensor that can be watched by a tape or passed to jax.grad.
concepts.misconception: The halves do not copy weights; they share the same layer objects as the original model.

concepts.name: Task preprocessor
concepts.definition: The preprocessing layer included in a KerasHub task, applied automatically by predict().
concepts.intuition: The model's built-in adapter from raw photos to network-ready tensors.
concepts.technical: model.preprocessor(img_array) applies it explicitly; needed because the Grad-CAM submodels start after preprocessing.
concepts.significance: Ensures the gradient computation sees the same input the network saw during prediction.
concepts.misconception: That predict() working on raw images means the submodels will too.

concepts.name: Functional API for feature extraction
concepts.definition: Creating a Keras Model from existing symbolic inputs and outputs of layers in another model.
concepts.intuition: Because layers are nodes in a graph, any node can become a model output.
concepts.technical: model.inputs and last_conv_layer.output are symbolic tensors from the already-built graph; keras.Model connects them.
concepts.significance: Lets you reuse a pretrained network's internals without retraining.
concepts.misconception: That you need to rebuild the architecture from scratch to get intermediate outputs.

deeper.title: Why split exactly at the last convolutional layer?
deeper.body:
- **Earlier layers** keep finer spatial detail, but their channels respond to edges and textures (p.322-p.323) rather than to object classes, so the heatmap would be less class-specific.
- **Later layers** (after global pooling) are class-specific but have no spatial axes: there is no 'where' left.
- **The last conv layer** is the deepest layer that still has a spatial grid, so it is the sweet spot.

This reasoning is an added explanation; the book simply chooses `block14_sepconv2_act`.

deeper.title: Composition check
deeper.body:
Once `classifier_model` is complete (p.326), you can verify the split:

1. `A = last_conv_layer_model(img_array)` (preprocessed input).
2. `p = classifier_model(A)`.
3. `p` should match `model.predict(raw_img_array)` up to numerical noise, and `argmax(p[0])` should be 386.

If it does not, preprocessing was probably skipped or applied twice. This is a suggested exercise, not in the book.

takeaways: The top five predictions are African elephant (90%), tusker (5%), Indian elephant (2%), triceratops and Mexican hairless dog (<0.1%).
The top class is index 386 (African elephant), found with np.argmax(preds[0]).
predict() preprocesses automatically; to use submodels directly, preprocess explicitly with model.preprocessor.
Listing 10.18 builds last_conv_layer_model from model.inputs to the output of block14_sepconv2_act in the backbone.
Listing 10.19 starts a second model whose input is that conv output, so the class score becomes a function of the feature map.

questions.question: What does np.argmax(preds[0]) return for the elephant image and what does it mean?
questions.answer: 386, the index of the African elephant class, which has the highest probability (about 0.90).
questions.explanation: Stated on the page; preds[0] is the 1,000-entry vector of the single image in the batch.

questions.question: Why does the book call img_array = model.preprocessor(img_array) before building the Grad-CAM models?
options: Because the submodels are called directly and do not apply the task's preprocessing, unlike predict()
To add a batch dimension to the image
To convert the image to grayscale for the heatmap
questions.answer: Because the submodels are called directly and do not apply the task's preprocessing, unlike predict()
questions.explanation: The page explains predict() preprocesses for us, so to use preprocessed inputs directly with the submodels we must do it ourselves. The batch dimension was added on p.323 with np.expand_dims; no grayscale conversion happens.

questions.question: Why is the model split at the last convolutional layer rather than at an early layer or after global pooling?
questions.answer: The last conv layer is the deepest layer that still has spatial dimensions: its channels encode high-level, class-relevant features, yet it still says where they occur. After pooling there is no spatial information; early layers are spatially precise but encode low-level patterns.
questions.explanation: This is an added explanation consistent with the book's Grad-CAM description (p.323) and the filter visualizations of section 10.2.

questions.question: In Listing 10.18, where is the layer block14_sepconv2_act looked up?
questions.explanation: The code calls model.backbone.get_layer(last_conv_layer_name). The preprocessor has no conv layers, keras.applications is not used, and classifier_model is built afterwards.

questions.question: The book says the network recognized 'an undetermined quantity of African elephants'. Why undetermined?
questions.answer: A classifier outputs a probability per class for the whole image; it has no output that counts instances. It only says African elephants are present.
questions.explanation: Counting or locating objects requires different models (object detection, chapter 12); Grad-CAM gives only a rough localization.

questions.question: If the last conv layer output has shape (1, 10, 10, 2048), how many numbers does the gradient tensor computed on the next page contain, and why that shape?
questions.answer: 204,800 (10 x 10 x 2048, plus the batch axis of size 1). The gradient of a scalar with respect to a tensor has the same shape as that tensor.
questions.explanation: The 10 x 10 x 2048 shape is a standard Xception value, not printed in the book; the rule that the gradient matches the shape of the variable applies regardless.

questions.question: Could you write Listing 10.18 for a different layer, say block13_sepconv2_act, and predict how the heatmap would change?
questions.answer: Replace the layer name; an earlier layer typically gives a finer-grained but less class-specific map.
questions.explanation: Self-check of understanding of model splitting; the trade-off reasoning is an added explanation.
